\paragraph{arXiv ($\Kempirical{=}3$): five-model cross-validation.}
All five domain-competent models yield $\Kempirical{=}3$ on arXiv, with boundary-pair $\auc$ (2v3) ranging from 0.6215 to 0.6545, all exceeding $\theta$.
The elevated signal reflects higher per-generation distributional shift (1v2 JSD $= 0.077$ vs.\ ${\sim}0.01$ for C4): formulaic features (LaTeX formatting, citation patterns, mathematical notation) degrade slowly under autoregressive generation and supply persistent depth signal across four architecture families and 1.4B--8B parameters.
Removing LaTeX markup reduces 2v3 AUC by ${\sim}$1.8\,pp but preserves $\Kempirical{=}3$ (CI lower $= 0.610 > \theta$; Table~\ref{tab:latex_ablation}); content-level properties dominate.
OLMo-1B is a capacity failure (0v1 JSD $= 0.33$, near-total information loss), not a counter-example.
Mistral-7B provides the strongest domain-dependence evidence: $\Kempirical{=}1$ on C4 (Section~\ref{sec:boundary_cases}) but $\Kempirical{=}3$ on arXiv: domain structure alone can shift $\Kempirical$ by two levels within the same model.

\paragraph{Wikipedia ($\Kempirical{=}1$): single-generation saturation.}
With scorer confound controlled (Pythia-1.4B for Qwen generators; Qwen-1.5B, itself cross-family, for all others), all six models yield $\Kempirical{=}1$ on Wikipedia: 1v2 $\auc$ ranges from 0.499 (OLMo) to 0.595 (LLaMA), all below $\theta$.
Wikipedia represents the simplest domain tested; its encyclopedic regularity provides minimal structural signal beyond the 0v1 boundary, and a single generation pass suffices for complete saturation.
Same-family scoring inflates Qwen $\Kempirical$ to 2 on Wikipedia ($\Delta = +2.4$\,pp); cross-family scoring controls this bias without affecting C4 results (Appendix~\ref{sec:wiki_domain}).

\paragraph{Code ($\Kempirical{=}1$--$2$): cross-modality confirmation.}
Python functions from CodeSearchNet~\cite{husain2019codesearchnet} ($n{=}5{,}000$) yield $\Kempirical{=}2$ for Qwen2.5-1.5B (1v2 $\auc = 0.738$; Table~\ref{tab:code_domain_qwen}), LLaMA-3.1-8B ($\auc = 0.739$), and Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($\auc = 0.615$, CI lower $= 0.603$; Table~\ref{tab:code_crossmodel_kstar}), but $\Kempirical{=}1$ for capacity-limited Pythia-1.4B ($\auc = 0.598$, CI upper $= 0.603$).
Code matches C4 despite a different modality, with the same sharp 2v3 collapse (JSD ratio $11.7$--$13.5\times$).
Cross-family scorer validation confirms Code $\Kempirical{=}2$ is text-intrinsic ($\Delta \leq 1.9$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:code_domain}).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
When models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This degradation arises in both \emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \emph{prompt-chains} (recursively generating from previous outputs without retraining); we study the latter, which isolates generation-level information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically and ignores the generational depth dimension.

This gap cuts across multiple communities.
Binary detectors~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp} produce no depth estimate (Section~\ref{sec:binary_confidence}).
Membership inference~\cite{zawalski2026codec} addresses a different question, and the model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} provides no per-text tool.
Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} likewise ignore recursive depth.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone.

Knowing whether the discriminable depth is finite, and where it saturates, has direct practical consequences.
For data curation, the saturation point determines filtering granularity: if discrimination collapses at depth 2, graduated weighting beyond that boundary injects noise, and binary filtering becomes the principled choice.
Model collapse theory predicts monotonic quality degradation across generations, but existing analyses are population-level and provide no per-text measure of where degradation saturates.
$\Kempirical$ fills this gap by localizing the generation at which adjacent outputs become empirically indistinguishable.

The Data Processing Inequality implies that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$; its actual value is determined empirically.
We empirically measure $\Kempirical$ (the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations) using 15 statistical features computed via a fixed reference scorer (Section~\ref{sec:features}) and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k \geq 1$ where the pairwise $\auc_{k-1,k}$ exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
  \item \textbf{First empirical measurement of $\Kempirical$} across 9 model configurations (5 architecture families, 1B--14B), 4 source domains (3 text + 1 code), and 4 decoding strategies at $\theta{=}0.60$: 4/5 families (8/9 configurations) yield $\Kempirical{=}2$ on C4 ($p \leq 0.002$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).

2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\begin{figure*}[t]
5	\centering
6	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/pipeline.pdf}
7	\caption{Generational depth estimation pipeline. Seed documents are recursively passed through a generation operator $G_\delta$ to produce a depth chain. Statistical features are fed to the OBD-LightGBM classifier for depth prediction.}
8	\label{fig:pipeline}
9	\end{figure*}
10	
11	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
12	\label{sec:formulation}
13	
14	A generation operator $G_\delta$ (LLM + decoding strategy $\delta$) produces successive generations $X \to Y_1 \to \cdots \to Y_K$, where $Y_k = G_\delta(Y_{k-1})$ and $Y_0 \triangleq X$ (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
15	This sequence forms a Markov chain.
16	By the Data Processing Inequality, $I(X; Y_1) \geq I(X; Y_2) \geq \cdots \geq 0$: the original signal degrades monotonically.
17	Together with Markov chain convergence, this motivates a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable; DPI guarantees existence but does not bound $\Ktheory$, so the actual saturation depth must be measured empirically.
18	
19	We define the operational lower bound:

% === Abstract ===
\begin{abstract}
Web-scale corpora are increasingly contaminated by recursive synthetic content, yet no method estimates a document's generational depth.
We measure the discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ (the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain distinguishable) using 15 statistical features and an OBD-LightGBM classifier.
Across five architecture families (1B--14B), four source domains (three text, one code), and four decoding strategies at $\theta{=}0.60$ (AUC decision threshold), $\Kempirical{=}2$ for general web text (8/9 model configurations), $\Kempirical{=}1$--$2$ for code (Python, model-dependent), and $\Kempirical{=}3$ for structured academic text (arXiv).
A single additional generation pass suffices to render first-generation synthetic web text indistinguishable from deeper synthetic content, a \emph{one-wash laundering} effect.
Largely generator-independent statistical features, computed via a fixed reference scorer, enable 80--92\% accuracy retention among continuation-mode generators, and cross-scorer validation confirms that $\Kempirical$ is largely robust to scorer choice.
Downstream, $\Kempirical$ characterizes discriminability boundaries that inform, but do not directly determine, filtering strategy; for web text ($\Kempirical{=}2$), binary filtering aligns with the two-level discriminability structure.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Limitations}

Our findings are bounded by:
(1)~\emph{Scope}: model scale $\leq$14B (5 architecture families), English text (C4, Wikipedia, arXiv) and Python code (CodeSearchNet), four decoding strategies; arXiv $\Kempirical{=}3$ is confirmed with five models across four architecture families but with reduced sample size ($n{=}2{,}200$ per model); code domain tested with five models across four families (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, $\Kempirical{=}2$; Pythia-1.4B, $\Kempirical{=}1$ with 1v2 CI upper bound $> \theta$); subsampling analysis indicates $n{\geq}2{,}000$ suffices for 100\% reliable $\Kempirical$ determination (Appendix~\ref{sec:power_curve}).
(2)~\emph{Protocol}: all main experiments use prompt-chain, which isolates text-intrinsic degradation from training dynamics; real-world contamination involves both prompting and retraining, and retrain-chain yields $\Kempirical{=}7$ (both Qwen-1.5B and Pythia-1.4B LoRA; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}), so prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ may underestimate discriminability in mixed settings.
(3)~\emph{Threshold}: $\Kempirical$ ranges from 2--3 at $\theta{=}0.55$ to 1 at $\theta{=}0.70$; 8/9 configurations yield $\Kempirical{=}2$ at $\theta{=}0.60$ (Mistral-7B: $\Kempirical{=}1$).
(4)~\emph{Marginal boundary}: Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.002; cross-scorer validation drops this to $\Kempirical{=}1$ (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}). LLaMA-3.1-8B (C4) and Mistral-7B-v0.3 (code) represent the most marginal $\Kempirical{=}2$ assignments, with 1v2 CI lower bounds within 0.3 percentage points of $\theta$.
(5)~\emph{Feature set}: the 15D features yield a feature-set-specific lower bound ($\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher); neural probe $\Kempirical$ is model-dependent ($3$ for Qwen, $2$ for Pythia/OLMo).
(6)~\emph{Segment length}: $\Kempirical{=}2$ confirmed for 128 and 256 tokens (CI lower $> \theta$); 512 tokens yields point estimate $\Kempirical{=}2$ but CI lower marginally below $\theta$ ($0.5979$); the boundary weakens at longer generation lengths.
(7)~\emph{Curation applicability}: the filtering evaluation is validated on two architectures (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Pythia-1.4B) with consistent strategy ordering (Appendix~\ref{sec:pythia_filtering}), though absolute improvement remains small and effect sizes diminish at lower contamination ratios (10--50\%; Appendix~\ref{sec:dose_response}).
(8)~\emph{Family balance}: the Qwen2.5 family provides 5/9 configurations; though spanning three scales (1.5B, 7B, 14B) and two training variants (base, instruct), aggregate statistics weight this family more heavily than the four single-configuration families.
Additional limitations (cross-model scoring sensitivity, feature ranking variability at the 1v2 boundary, structural composition confound analysis) appear in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

Generational depth estimation is intended for data curation and corpus auditing, positive-sum applications that improve training data quality.
Our experiments use publicly available corpora (C4, Wikipedia, arXiv abstracts) and do not involve personally identifiable information.
A potential dual-use concern is that depth estimation techniques could inform adversarial strategies to evade detection (e.g., by calibrating rewriting to mimic earlier-generation statistics); we note that this risk is shared by all detection research and that the binary detection boundary ($\auc \geq 0.96$ at 0v1) remains robust.
Code and generated corpora will be released upon acceptance to enable reproducibility.
